title: Executable eval case
description: AUTHORING.md §9. The `evals/<skill-id>/<case-id>/case.yaml` that the host's eval runner loads, as against the `tests[]` entry in skill.yaml that declares it. This schema says a case is **well-formed**. It does not say a case is covered, or tested, or that it passes: nothing in this package executes a case, and that is by design -- `adapters/runner-contract/CONTRACT.md` §1 puts execution, isolation and credentials with the runner, and the plan hands the running of these files to `claude plugin eval` on the host. Before this existed a `case.yaml` reduced to a single `tags:` line validated exactly as the full case beside it did, and an empty file was a valid case that satisfied `evals.declaration-without-case` and counted toward the three-case floor. That is what this closes, and it is all of what it closes. A case is configuration, not a durable run artifact, so it carries no envelope and is absent from common.schema.json#/$defs/schema_id.

schema_version.description: The loader's case format, not this package's version -- AUTHORING.md §8 keeps the two independent. Pinned to the one format this schema was written against, so a host that starts emitting a newer one is a deliberate edit here rather than a silent divergence between what the runner accepts and what this file describes.

name.description: The case's own name, which is not the directory name: the directory equals the `tests[].id` that declares it and is the join `ak validate` checks, while this reads as a sentence about the behavior.

tags.description: Case kind and release-scenario claims. Deliberately unconstrained beyond shape: which kinds a skill must carry is `REQUIRED_CASE_KINDS` in src/validation/evals.ts, and which `scenario-NN` values name a real scenario is `evals.scenario-tag-out-of-range` in the same file. Both are checks with messages that explain themselves, and an enum here would be a second, mute copy of them that could disagree.

execution.description:
What the runner is asked to do. Closed, but on the keys the host reads rather than on the three AUTHORING.md §9 happens to document.

It was closed on those three, with the reason that a key the loader accepts and this does not is "a schema edit, which is the direction that gets noticed". That reasoning was wrong and is recorded here rather than deleted, because the way it failed is the point. It was not noticed and could not have been: the symptom of refusing a key the host accepts is that nobody writes that key, and the one author who tries gets a validation error naming their own file and concludes they were mistaken. A closed schema fails by making the missing feature look like nothing anyone wanted. `scaffold_script` was refused from 7db25a7 until it was declared here, and the visible result was a corpus in which no case declared a fixture and a run that scored 0.00 against an empty workspace.

The keys here have two owners. `prompt` is this package's. `max_turns`, `allowed_tools` and `timeout_seconds` are the host's, settled elsewhere, and no amount of internal agreement between §9, this file and src/ is evidence about them -- which is why each one names the host version it was confirmed against. `allowed_tools` already said as much about its members and this file then closed the object against the host's other keys, which is the same mistake one level up.

prompt.description: The prompt the case runs. Required, and non-empty, because a case whose prompt is absent is the stub this schema exists to refuse.

max_turns.description: A cap the runner enforces. An integer count with no currency and no tier, like every other limit in this package.

allowed_tools.description: The tools the run may use. Not enumerated here: the set is the host's, and a case that needs a tool this package has never heard of is the host's business rather than a defect in the case.

timeout_seconds.description: Wall-clock seconds for the run, bounding it alongside `max_turns`. Beside `max_turns` here because the host documents the two as siblings. An under-set value scores 0 rather than reporting a timeout, which is the failure mode worth knowing about: it reads as the skill having done nothing. Host-owned, on two independent receipts: `claude plugin eval --help` at claude 2.1.278, and the authoring spec `claude plugin eval init` prints, which names it in the `prompt.md` frontmatter list. The receipt covers the key's existence and its meaning, not its position in a `case.yaml` -- the host's own `init --bare` writes `prompt.md` frontmatter, and this file's arrangement of the same keys is this package's.

graders.description: How the run is scored. At least one, because a case that grades nothing cannot fail and is therefore not a case.

items.description: Open, not closed, and that is a known divergence from the host rather than a safe default. AUTHORING.md §9 lists five grader types and documents the fields of three: `tool` for `tool_used`, `pattern` for `regex`, `criteria` for `llm`. Those three names are no longer read from §9 -- they are what `claude plugin eval` accepted at `claude 2.1.278`, measured by loading the whole corpus against it. §9 said `expected_outcome` for `llm`, this schema required it, all 256 `llm` graders carried it, and the host rejects that key outright: 87 of 87 shipped cases failed to load, and none of them had ever been run. What `file_exists`, `tool_order` and `baseline` take is no longer unknown: 4756a2e read it off the host binary's loader definition and §9 now states it. `research/probes/host-case-keys.py` reconciles this object against a different source, the authoring spec `claude plugin eval init` prints, and reports that it names none of `regex`'s `target`/`match`/`flags`, none of `llm`'s `focus`, and none of `tool_used`'s `input_match`/`min`/`max`/`arm`. The two sources are each incomplete in the other's direction -- the loader definition carries the signatures and not the defaults, the authoring spec carries the defaults and lists five grader types where the loader has six -- so neither is a proof of agreement and the probe reports a floor. The object nonetheless stays open here. Declaring those fields is a contract change that belongs with §9 and is filed at CONTRACT-DEFECTS.md rather than settled by a schema edit, and the entry says why: `focus` defaults to `last_message`, so the 41 `llm` graders in this tree that assert something about the filesystem are scored against the transcript, and naming the key without ruling on those graders would look like a fix. But **the host's grader object is closed** -- it refuses any key it does not define, which is how two surplus `expected_outcome` fields on `tool_used` graders were caught. So the openness here buys no safety against the runner: it postpones one guess and admits exactly the surplus the runner will reject.

type.description: The six types AUTHORING.md §9 lists. `baseline` was absent from this enum until 4756a2e measured it off the host binary's loader definition, which meant a `baseline` grader was refused here -- the same shape as `scaffold_script`, and missed for the same reason: an enum that omits a value produces no artifact naming it. `research/probes/host-case-keys.py` did not catch this one either, because its source is the authoring spec `claude plugin eval init` prints and that spec's table lists five types. The loader definition is the stronger source for grader fields; the authoring spec is the only source for their defaults. Neither alone is complete. §9 also asks for a deterministic grader over `llm` wherever the pass criterion is observable, which is a preference a schema cannot hold.

allOf.description: An `llm` grader is its `criteria` -- §9 asks for one 'that a reader could score by hand', and without it there is nothing for a judge to read. The host requires this exact key and reports a grader missing it as `graders.N.criteria: Required`.

A `tool_used` grader that names no tool asserts nothing about any tool. It is the eval-case form of a locator that matches no instance: it cannot fail, so it cannot grade, and nothing in this package would ever have said so because nothing here runs it. Inferred from §9's worked example, which carries `tool: Skill`, rather than measured against the loader, for the reason this object is open.
Same shape for the pattern a `regex` grader matches.

scaffold_script.description: Author-supplied bash that stages the workspace before the run, executed only under `--scaffold` and skipped under `--no-scaffold`; `--keep-temp` preserves what it built. At the case root rather than in `execution` because it prepares what the run starts from rather than saying what the runner is asked to do. Optional: a case that needs no fixture declares none, and until this key was declared here a case that needed one could not be written at all -- `ak validate` refused it, so the corpus reads as though no case ever wanted a fixture. Host-owned: confirmed against `claude plugin eval --help` at claude 2.1.278, and confirmed there only. It is absent from the authoring spec `claude plugin eval init` prints, which states its own completeness but is complete about `prompt.md` frontmatter rather than about everything a case can carry. That asymmetry is why `research/probes/host-case-keys.py` reports a floor on divergence and not agreement: the two enumerations each omit something the other has, so neither alone would have found this key. The receipt covers the key's existence and its meaning, not its position in a `case.yaml` -- the host's own `init --bare` writes `prompt.md` frontmatter, and this file's arrangement of the same keys is this package's.

runs.description: How many times the host runs this case, defaulting to 3 when absent and overridden by `--runs`. Spelled `case.runs` in the host's own help, which is why it sits at the root. An integer count with no currency and no tier, like every other limit in this package. Host-owned, on two independent receipts: `claude plugin eval --help` at claude 2.1.278, and the authoring spec `claude plugin eval init` prints, which names it in the `prompt.md` frontmatter list and states its default of 3. The second is the stronger of the two -- a help text mentions what it happens to mention, so absence from it is not evidence, whereas the spec states its own completeness. The receipt covers the key's existence and its meaning, not its position in a `case.yaml` -- the host's own `init --bare` writes `prompt.md` frontmatter, and this file's arrangement of the same keys is this package's.
